_note: The first ten apps. Every factual field is taken from the app's own website and its Apple and Google listings, checked on 16 September 2026, and the sources are recorded per app. Editorial fields — tagline, take, what we like, things to consider — are ours and say who an app suits rather than what it will do for anybody. Prices are deliberately sparse: an app that publishes no price gets an empty field and 'see the app for pricing' on the card, because a wrong price is worse than none. Everything imports as a draft for review.

apps.title: Calm
apps.tagline: Sleep stories, meditations and background sound, in one calm-feeling app.
apps.excerpt: One of the two best-known meditation apps, built as much around sleep as around meditation. Guided sessions sit alongside Sleep Stories read by well-known voices, breathing exercises and a large library of ambient sound. It is a polished, gentle place to start, and most of it sits behind a subscription.
apps.pricing_notes: Free to download, with a subscription for most content. Calm does not publish its Australian price on its own site, so check the price in the app store before subscribing.
apps.take: Calm suits someone who wants the wind-down more than the discipline: sleep stories, sound and short guided sessions in an app that is genuinely nice to open at night. If you want a structured course that teaches you to meditate, Headspace is the better fit.
features: Guided meditations for sleep, stress and focus
Sleep Stories read by well-known narrators
Breathing exercises and ambient soundscapes
Short daily sessions for building a habit
pros: The sleep content is the strongest of any mainstream meditation app
Calm, uncluttered design that suits people new to this
Sessions short enough to fit into an ordinary evening
cons: Most of the library needs a subscription
Less structured than a course-based app if you want to learn technique

faq.question: Is Calm free?
faq.answer: The app is free to download and includes some free content, but the bulk of the library, including most Sleep Stories, requires a subscription.

faq.question: Is Calm good for sleep?
faq.answer: Sleep is what it is best known for. Sleep Stories, ambient sound and wind-down sessions are all designed to be used at bedtime, and many people use it for nothing else.

apps.title: Headspace
apps.tagline: Structured meditation courses for people who want to be taught, not just guided.
apps.excerpt: Headspace teaches meditation as a skill, through courses that build in order rather than a library you browse. Alongside the meditation it carries sleepcasts and wind-downs, short mindfulness exercises for the middle of a working day, and in some markets coaching and therapy. Everything beyond the trial needs a subscription.
apps.pricing_notes: Headspace advertises a 14-day free trial, then monthly or annual billing, with student and family plans. The Australian price is not published on its site; check in the app store.
apps.take: The one to choose if you have tried meditating and bounced off it. The courses are ordered, the instruction is plain, and the sessions are short enough that starting is not a decision. Less useful if you already have a practice and just want a big library to wander through.
features: Ordered courses that teach meditation from the beginning
Sleepcasts and wind-down audio for bedtime
Short exercises for focus during the day
Over a thousand expert-led sessions
pros: The clearest teaching of any of the mainstream apps
Short sessions make a daily habit realistic
Sleep content included rather than sold separately
cons: No free tier beyond the trial
The structure that helps beginners can feel restrictive once you have a practice

faq.question: Is Headspace free?
faq.answer: No. There is a 14-day free trial, after which it is a paid subscription. A handful of sessions stay available outside the trial.

faq.question: Is Headspace good for beginners?
faq.answer: It is the most beginner-oriented of the well-known apps. The courses run in order and explain what you are doing and why, rather than handing you a library to sort through.

apps.title: Insight Timer
apps.tagline: An enormous free library of guided meditation, and a timer for practising on your own.
apps.excerpt: Insight Timer is the opposite of a course: hundreds of thousands of free tracks from thousands of teachers, including a number of Australian ones, plus live sessions and a plain meditation timer with interval bells. The free tier is unusually generous, which makes it the natural first app to try.
apps.pricing_notes: The library is free. A paid membership adds courses and offline listening; the price is not published on the site, so check in the app store.
apps.take: If you are not sure meditation is for you, start here rather than paying for anything. The free library is vast and the timer is genuinely useful once you practise on your own. The other side of that size is that browsing can become its own form of procrastination.
features: A very large free library of guided meditations
Meditation timer with interval bells for unguided practice
Live sessions and teacher-led events
Sleep audio, music and yoga nidra
pros: The most generous free tier of any meditation app
Australian teachers among the thousands on the platform
The timer suits people who already know how to sit
cons: Quality varies from teacher to teacher, because anyone can publish
The size of the library can be its own obstacle when starting out

faq.question: Is Insight Timer really free?
faq.answer: The main library is free to use. A paid membership adds features such as courses and offline listening, but the meditations themselves do not sit behind it.

faq.question: What is the timer for?
faq.answer: It is for meditating without guidance: you set a length and interval bells, and the app stays out of the way. It is the feature experienced meditators tend to use most.

apps.title: Smiling Mind
apps.tagline: An Australian not-for-profit mindfulness app, free for everyone, including programs for children.
apps.excerpt: Smiling Mind is made by an Australian not-for-profit and has stayed free for individuals and families for over a decade. It runs as ordered programs rather than a library, with pathways for adults and separate ones written for children, and a schools program behind it.
apps.pricing_notes: Free. Smiling Mind is a not-for-profit and states the app has remained free for individuals and families for over twelve years.
apps.take: The one to recommend to a family. It is Australian, it is free with nothing held back, and the children's pathways are written for children rather than being adult sessions with a softer voice. For an adult wanting depth, the library is smaller than the paid apps.
features: Over 700 sessions across 90 collections and pathways
Separate programs for children, teenagers and adults
Routines and progress tracking
Content on sleep, stress and managing emotions
pros: Genuinely free, from a not-for-profit, with no upsell
Made in Australia, including a widely used schools program
Among the few mindfulness apps written properly for children
cons: A smaller library than the large subscription apps
Less polished than Calm or Headspace in places

faq.question: Is Smiling Mind free?
faq.answer: Yes. It is run by an Australian not-for-profit and has been free for individuals and families for more than twelve years.

faq.question: Is Smiling Mind suitable for children?
faq.answer: Yes. It has pathways written specifically for children and teenagers, and the same organisation runs a mindfulness program used in Australian schools.

apps.title: BetterSleep
apps.tagline: Mix your own sleep soundscape, with stories and wind-down audio alongside.
apps.excerpt: BetterSleep, formerly Relax Melodies, is built around sound: you layer rain, fans, white noise and instruments into a mix of your own, and it plays as you fall asleep. Around that sit narrated sleep stories, meditations and breathing exercises. The app is free to use, with a good deal of the content behind a subscription.
apps.pricing_notes: Free to download and use, with much of the content requiring the Premium plan. The Australian price is not published on the site; check in the app store.
apps.take: The one for people who sleep better with sound. Being able to build the mix yourself, rather than picking from fixed tracks, is what makes it different from the meditation apps that bolt sleep audio on the side.
features: Custom sound mixing from a large library of sounds
Narrated sleep stories
Sleep meditations and breathing exercises
Binaural beats and ASMR content
pros: The sound mixing is genuinely better than its rivals
Usable free, unlike the big subscription apps
Good for shift workers and light sleepers who need masking sound
cons: The best content sits behind the Premium plan
Sound all night affects phone battery unless it is charging

faq.question: Is BetterSleep free?
faq.answer: The app is free to download and use, but not all content is available without the Premium plan.

faq.question: What happened to Relax Melodies?
faq.answer: It was renamed. BetterSleep is the same app with the same sound library.

apps.title: Sleep Cycle
apps.tagline: Tracks your sleep by sound and wakes you at a lighter point in the cycle.
apps.excerpt: A Swedish app that listens rather than needing a wearable: it analyses sound through the night, scores your sleep on duration, quality and consistency, and wakes you inside a window rather than at an exact minute. It suits people who want to see patterns over months rather than fiddle with settings.
apps.pricing_notes: Sleep Cycle advertises a free trial, but its own site shows two different lengths in different places, and no Australian price. Check both the trial length and the price in the app store before subscribing.
apps.take: Useful if you suspect your sleep is worse than it feels and want evidence over time. It needs no watch, which is the practical advantage. Treat the score as a trend line rather than a measurement, and do not let checking it become the thing that keeps you awake.
features: Sleep tracking by sound analysis, no wearable needed
Smart alarm that wakes you within a chosen window
A nightly sleep score from duration, quality and routine
Long-run trends and statistics
pros: Works with just a phone beside the bed
Long history makes patterns visible over months
The waking window is gentler than a fixed alarm
cons: The trial length is advertised inconsistently on their own site
Sleep scores can become something to worry about rather than act on

faq.question: Does Sleep Cycle need a smartwatch?
faq.answer: No. It analyses sound with the phone beside the bed, which is the main practical difference from wearable-based trackers.

faq.question: Is Sleep Cycle free?
faq.answer: There is a free trial, then a subscription. The site advertises different trial lengths in different places, so check before you sign up.

apps.title: FitOn
apps.tagline: Free workout videos across cardio, strength, yoga and pilates.
apps.excerpt: FitOn offers unlimited free workout videos, which is unusual in fitness apps: cardio, strength, pilates, yoga, toning and meditation, with programs you can follow rather than one-off sessions. A paid tier adds meal plans and extra content, but the workouts themselves are free.
apps.pricing_notes: The workout library is free. A paid tier adds meal plans and extra content; the price is not published on the site, so check in the app store.
apps.take: The obvious first stop if you want to train at home without paying anything. The range is broad rather than deep, which suits someone building a habit more than someone chasing a specific programme.
features: Free workout videos across cardio, strength, pilates and yoga
Multi-week programs rather than only single sessions
Meditation and recovery content alongside the workouts
Challenges and social features for motivation
pros: A genuinely free workout library, which is rare
Enough variety to keep a home routine interesting
Short sessions for days when a full workout will not happen
cons: Meal plans and some content need the paid tier
Less specialised than a dedicated strength or running app

faq.question: Is FitOn free?
faq.answer: The workout library is free and unlimited. A paid tier adds meal plans and extra content.

faq.question: Do I need equipment?
faq.answer: Many of the workouts are bodyweight only, with equipment-based sessions marked so you can filter them out.

apps.title: Nike Training Club
apps.tagline: Over 200 workouts from Nike trainers, free, from five minutes to fifty.
apps.excerpt: Nike Training Club gives away what used to be a paid library: more than 200 workouts led by Nike trainers, covering strength, HIIT, yoga, cardio and mobility, with multi-week programs for people who want structure. Sessions run from five to fifty minutes, so it fits days when there is no time as well as days when there is.
apps.pricing_notes: Free to download and use. Nike states the workouts and programs are free.
apps.take: The best-produced free workout app there is, and the five-minute mobility sessions do more for most people than the hard ones. Worth having installed even if you train elsewhere.
features: More than 200 free workouts led by Nike trainers
Four to six week programs for structure
Strength, HIIT, yoga, cardio and mobility
Apple Watch support and progress tracking
pros: Free, with no tier held back
Production and coaching quality above most paid apps
Short sessions make it usable on a bad week
cons: Workout planning tools are richer on iPhone than on Android
Built around Nike, so expect the brand throughout

faq.question: Is Nike Training Club free?
faq.answer: Yes. Nike makes the workouts and programs free to download and use.

faq.question: Is it only for people who already train?
faq.answer: No. Sessions start at five minutes and include mobility and beginner strength, though it assumes you can follow a video without hands-on correction.

apps.title: Strava
apps.tagline: Records your runs, rides and walks, and makes them social.
apps.excerpt: Strava tracks activity by GPS and turns it into something shared: routes, segments, clubs and challenges, with friends able to see and respond to what you did. For a lot of people the social side is the point, and it is what keeps them going out. The core is free, with a subscription for the deeper analysis.
apps.pricing_notes: Free to join and use, with a paid subscription for extra analysis and route features. The Australian price is not published on the site; check in the app store.
apps.take: Worth it for the accountability more than the data. If seeing that a friend went out this morning is what gets you out the door, this is the app that does it. If comparing yourself to other people is not motivating for you, it is the wrong one.
features: GPS tracking for running, riding, walking and thirty other sports
Segments and routes for exploring
Clubs and challenges
Beacon, which shares your live location with a safety contact
pros: The social side is genuinely motivating for a lot of people
Works with most GPS watches rather than locking you in
Beacon is a real safety feature for running alone
cons: The comparison and leaderboards do not suit everyone
Some analysis is subscription-only
Worth checking your privacy settings before recording from home

faq.question: Is Strava free?
faq.answer: Yes, it is free to join and record activities. A subscription adds deeper analysis and route planning.

faq.question: Is Strava only for runners and cyclists?
faq.answer: No. It records walking, hiking, swimming, yoga and more than thirty other activities, though running and cycling are where its features are deepest.

apps.title: AllTrails
apps.tagline: Finds walks and trails near you, with maps that work without reception.
apps.excerpt: AllTrails is a map of walking, hiking and running trails, with reviews and photographs from people who have been. Downloadable maps mean navigation keeps working where there is no phone reception, which in the hills around Perth is the feature that matters. The basics are free, with a paid tier for offline maps.
apps.pricing_notes: Free to browse and record. Offline maps and some navigation features need the paid tier; the Australian price is not published on the site, so check in the app store.
apps.take: The easiest way to find a walk you have not done before, and the reviews are honest about what a trail is actually like underfoot. If you walk in the hills or anywhere past reception, the offline maps are the reason to pay.
features: Trail maps with reviews and photographs from walkers
Live tracking and activity recaps
Offline map downloads for areas without reception
Custom route building
pros: Finds walks near you that you would not otherwise know about
Reviews are specific about conditions and difficulty
Offline maps are a genuine safety feature outside reception
cons: Offline maps sit behind the paid tier
Trail information is community-written, so conditions can be out of date

faq.question: Is AllTrails free?
faq.answer: Browsing trails and recording walks is free. Offline maps and some navigation features require the paid tier.

faq.question: Does it work where there is no reception?
faq.answer: Only if you download the map before you go, which requires the paid tier. Without that, navigation needs a signal.

apps.title: Down Dog
apps.tagline: Builds a different yoga practice every time, at the level and length you choose.
apps.excerpt: Rather than a library of filmed classes, Down Dog generates a new sequence each time you start: you set the style, the level, the pace and how long you have, and it builds the practice around that. It suits people who want to practise often without working through a fixed course, and beginners who would rather not walk into a room first.
apps.pricing_notes: There is a usable free version with fewer options, and a subscription that unlocks the rest. Down Dog also sells a bundle covering its other apps, so check which one you are buying before you subscribe.
apps.take: The one to try if a fixed video course has put you off before. Because it builds a new sequence each time, you can practise daily for months without repeating yourself, and the beginner levels genuinely start at the beginning. It talks you through poses rather than showing a person to copy, which suits some people and not others.
features: A newly generated sequence each session rather than fixed videos
Over ten styles, including restorative, yin and vinyasa
Beginner levels that unlock more poses as you go
Choose the length, pace, voice and focus area before you start
pros: Practices never repeat, so it survives daily use
The beginner setting is genuinely beginner level
Works offline once a practice is downloaded
cons: Generated sequences can feel less considered than a taught class
The family of Down Dog apps is sold in several ways, which takes reading

faq.question: Is Down Dog good for beginners?
faq.answer: Yes. Beginner 1 assumes no experience and introduces poses gradually as you practise, which is the main reason people pick it over a video library.

faq.question: Is Down Dog free?
faq.answer: There is a free version with a smaller set of options. The full range of styles, lengths and boosts needs a subscription.

faq.question: Do I need equipment?
faq.answer: A mat is enough for most practices. Some styles suggest blocks or a bolster, and the app offers alternatives where you have none.

apps.title: Pacer
apps.tagline: Counts your steps from your pocket, without a wearable or a subscription to start.
apps.excerpt: A step counter that uses the phone you already carry, with walking groups, challenges and GPS route recording alongside. It suits people who want to walk more and see it add up, rather than people training for anything in particular.
apps.pricing_notes: Step counting, groups and challenges work without paying. Pacer Premium adds plans and deeper statistics; check the price in the app store, as it is not published as an Australian figure on their site.
apps.take: The easiest first step for somebody who wants to move more and does not want a project. It counts what you were going to do anyway, the free version is genuinely usable, and nothing about it assumes you are training. The group challenges are the part that keeps people going.
features: Counts steps from the phone in your pocket or bag
Walking groups and challenges with friends or strangers
GPS recording for walks, with routes and maps
Syncs with Apple Health and Apple Watch
pros: No wearable needed, and no subscription to get started
Works the same whether your friends are on iPhone or Android
Simple enough to hand to someone who dislikes apps
cons: Phone-based step counts are approximate, not a measurement
The free version pushes Premium fairly often

faq.question: Do I need a smartwatch for Pacer?
faq.answer: No. It counts steps using the phone's own sensors, whether the phone is in your hand, pocket or bag. It will also sync with an Apple Watch if you have one.

faq.question: Is Pacer free?
faq.answer: Yes, for step counting, groups and challenges. A Premium subscription adds guided plans and more detailed statistics.

faq.question: Does it drain the battery?
faq.answer: Ordinary step counting uses the phone's low-power motion sensor rather than GPS. Recording a walk with GPS uses considerably more.

apps.title: Runna
apps.tagline: A structured running plan built around your goal race, week by week.
apps.excerpt: Runna writes you a running plan — 5k through to ultra — and tells you what to run each day, with the session on your watch and the results synced to Strava. It suits somebody who has been running without a plan and has stopped improving, more than somebody deciding whether to start.
apps.free_trial: Runna advertises a free trial; check the current length in the app store
apps.pricing_notes: A subscription with no free tier. Runna was bought by Strava, so a Strava subscription may change what you pay — worth checking both before you sign up to either.
apps.take: Worth it if you run already and want to be told what to do rather than deciding each morning. The plans adapt, the watch integration means you are not reading your phone mid-run, and it is genuinely good at building toward a date. If you are not sure you will still be running in a month, start with something free.
features: Plans for 5k through to ultra, built around a goal date
Daily sessions with intervals sent to a running watch
Plans adjust as your paces change
Syncs finished runs to Strava
pros: Removes the daily decision about what to run
Watch-first, so the phone stays at home
Plans genuinely adapt rather than just counting down
cons: No free tier at all, so the trial is the only way to judge it
More structure than a casual runner is likely to want

faq.question: Is Runna free?
faq.answer: No. There is a free trial and then a subscription; there is no ongoing free tier.

faq.question: Do I need a running watch?
faq.answer: No, but it is better with one. Sessions can be sent to a watch so you are not looking at a phone during intervals.

faq.question: Does Runna work with Strava?
faq.answer: Yes. Completed runs sync to Strava, and Strava now owns Runna, so check whether a subscription to one affects the other.

apps.title: Nike Run Club
apps.tagline: Free guided runs with a voice in your ear, and a tracker underneath.
apps.excerpt: A free running app with several hundred guided runs — a coach talking you through the session as you go — plus training plans, distance tracking and challenges with other people. It suits somebody starting to run, or anybody who finds a voice easier to follow than a watch face.
apps.pricing_notes: Free, including the guided runs and training plans. It asks you to create a Nike account, which is also how Nike markets to you.
apps.take: The best free way to start running, because the guided runs mean somebody is telling you what to do and why while you do it. The first-run sessions are genuinely aimed at people who have never run. Expect the shop to be one tap away — it is a free app because Nike sells shoes.
features: Several hundred guided runs, free, from short first runs upward
Training plans building toward 5k, 10k or a half marathon
Distance, pace and route tracking, with an Apple Watch app
Challenges and leaderboards with friends
pros: Free, with no paid tier holding back the good parts
The guided runs suit absolute beginners better than most paid plans
Works on the watch without carrying a phone
cons: It is marketing as well as an app, and asks for a Nike account
Less adaptable than a paid plan once you are past the basics

faq.question: Is Nike Run Club actually free?
faq.answer: Yes. The guided runs and training plans are free; you need a Nike account, which also signs you up to their marketing unless you opt out.

faq.question: Is it any good for a complete beginner?
faq.answer: It is one of the better options. The first guided runs assume you have never run and talk you through walking and running intervals.

faq.question: Does it work with Apple Watch?
faq.answer: Yes, including runs recorded on the watch alone without the phone.

apps.title: komoot
apps.tagline: Plans walks and rides on real surfaces, and navigates them out loud.
apps.excerpt: A route planner that knows the difference between a sealed path and a rough trail, with turn-by-turn voice navigation and offline maps once a region is downloaded. It suits people who want to plan a walk or ride properly before leaving, and follow it without reception.
apps.pricing_notes: Planning and one map region are free; more regions and the premium features are paid. komoot changed hands in 2025 and its pricing has moved since, so check what is included before buying anything.
apps.take: The planner is the reason to have it: you can see before you leave whether a route is gravel, singletrack or footpath, which matters far more on a long walk than the distance does. Offline maps make it the sensible choice once you are past reception. Its pricing has been in flux, so read what you are buying.
features: Route planning by surface and difficulty, not just distance
Turn-by-turn voice navigation on trails as well as roads
Offline maps for a downloaded region
Routes and photos shared by other people who have done them
pros: Honest about what a path is actually like underfoot
Planning on a big screen, walking from the phone
Community routes are useful in unfamiliar country
cons: Pricing has changed since the company was sold, so check before buying
Australian trail coverage is thinner than in Europe

faq.question: Is komoot free?
faq.answer: Planning routes is free and one map region is included. Further regions and premium features cost extra, and that pricing has changed recently.

faq.question: Does komoot work without phone reception?
faq.answer: Yes, once you have downloaded the region and saved the route. That is the main reason people choose it for remote walks.

faq.question: Is it only for cycling?
faq.answer: No. It plans walking, running, hiking and cycling, and the surface information is arguably most useful on foot.

apps.title: Bend
apps.tagline: Short guided stretching routines, with a free set that is enough on its own.
apps.excerpt: A stretching app built around short routines — five or ten minutes for the lower back, hips, neck or a full body sequence — with a timer and a diagram for each stretch. It suits people who sit all day, and anyone easing back into movement who wants something gentler than a workout app.
apps.pricing_notes: A set of routines is free and usable indefinitely. A subscription unlocks the rest and removes the reminders to upgrade; the price is not published as an Australian figure, so check the app store.
apps.take: The gentlest thing on this list, and the one most likely to actually get used, because five minutes is a low bar. It suits people who are not looking for a workout at all — after a desk day, before bed, or easing back into moving. The free routines are enough to tell whether you will keep it.
features: Short routines by body area — back, hips, neck, full body
A timer and a diagram for every stretch
Reminders, if you want them, at a time you choose
Routines from a few minutes upward
pros: Five-minute routines are short enough to do on a bad day
The free set is genuinely usable rather than a sampler
No workout framing, which suits people put off by fitness apps
cons: Diagrams rather than video, which some people find harder to follow
The free version prompts you to upgrade fairly regularly

faq.question: Is Bend free?
faq.answer: A set of routines is free and stays free. A subscription unlocks the full library and removes the upgrade prompts.

faq.question: Is it suitable if I am not very flexible?
faq.answer: Yes — the routines are built around short, ordinary stretches rather than positions that assume existing flexibility, and each has a diagram and a timer.

faq.question: How long does a routine take?
faq.answer: Most are between five and fifteen minutes, and you choose the length before you start.

apps.title: Breathwrk
apps.tagline: Guided breathing exercises with a visual, a sound and a haptic to follow.
apps.excerpt: A breathing app with short exercises grouped by what you want from them — winding down, waking up, steadying yourself before something — where the phone shows, sounds and vibrates the rhythm so you are not counting. Now owned by Peloton, and included with a Peloton membership.
apps.pricing_notes: Some exercises are free; the rest need a subscription. Peloton All Access, Guide and App+ members get it included, so check your existing memberships before paying twice.
apps.take: The useful thing here is the haptic: the phone vibrates the rhythm, so you can put it in a pocket and follow a breathing pattern without counting or watching a screen. Exercises run from about a minute, which is short enough to use before something rather than instead of it. The free set is small.
features: Short exercises grouped by sleep, calm, energy and focus
A visual, a sound and a haptic to breathe along to
Exercises from around a minute upward
Customisable pattern length for people who know what they want
pros: The haptic means you can follow it without looking at the screen
Short enough to use in the moment rather than as a session
Included at no extra cost for existing Peloton members
cons: The free set is limited compared with the subscription
Peloton's ownership means more cross-promotion than there used to be

faq.question: Is Breathwrk free?
faq.answer: Some exercises are free and a subscription unlocks the rest. Peloton All Access, Guide and App+ members have it included with their membership.

faq.question: How long does an exercise take?
faq.answer: Most run from about a minute to a few minutes, which is the point — they are meant to fit into a day rather than be scheduled.

faq.question: Do I need to watch the screen?
faq.answer: No. The phone can vibrate the rhythm, so it works in a pocket or with the screen face down.

apps.title: Forest
apps.tagline: Plant a tree that dies if you pick up your phone.
apps.excerpt: A focus timer with one idea behind it: start a session and a tree grows on screen, leave the app early and it withers. Sessions build a forest over time, and the company has a partnership that plants real trees. It suits people whose problem is the phone itself rather than the work.
apps.pricing_notes: Usable without paying, with in-app purchases for extra trees and features. Check the app store for the current cost of the paid extras.
apps.take: A gimmick that works, which is the only test that matters. Not wanting to kill a cartoon tree turns out to be a stronger deterrent than willpower for a lot of people, and the forest you build up is a record of attention rather than of hours. If a plain timer already works for you, you do not need this.
features: A focus timer where leaving the app kills the tree
A growing record of sessions over weeks and months
Allow-lists for apps you genuinely need during a session
A partnership that plants real trees
pros: Makes leaving the app feel like a cost, which is the whole trick
The long view is a record of attention, not just time
Works without an account or a subscription
cons: Does nothing about distraction that is not on your phone
The gamification wears off for some people after a few weeks

faq.question: Is Forest free?
faq.answer: Yes, with in-app purchases for extra features and tree varieties. The core timer works without paying.

faq.question: Does Forest really plant trees?
faq.answer: The company runs a partnership under which coins earned in the app fund real tree planting. The planting is done by the partner organisation, not by Forest.

faq.question: What happens if I need another app mid-session?
faq.answer: You can allow specific apps so using them does not kill the tree. Anything outside that list does.

apps.title: Endel
apps.tagline: Generated sound that keeps going, for focus, winding down or sleep.
apps.excerpt: Endel makes continuous soundscapes rather than playing tracks, shifting with the time of day and what you have asked it for — focus, relax, sleep or movement. It suits people who work better with sound but find music distracting, and anybody who wants something that does not end.
apps.pricing_notes: A limited amount is free and full access is a subscription. Endel does not publish an Australian price on its own site, so check the figure in the app store before subscribing.
apps.take: Worth trying if music with structure pulls your attention but silence is worse. Because the sound is generated rather than looped, it does not end or repeat in a way you notice, which is the practical difference from a playlist. Whether that is worth a subscription depends entirely on how much of the day you would use it.
features: Continuous generated soundscapes rather than fixed tracks
Modes for focus, relaxing, sleep and moving
Shifts with time of day and inputs from the phone
An Apple Watch app for starting it without the phone
pros: Never ends or loops noticeably, unlike a playlist
Less attention-grabbing than music with structure
Sleep and focus in one app rather than two subscriptions
cons: The free tier is limited enough that the subscription is the real product
Generated sound is a matter of taste — some people find it sterile

faq.question: Is Endel free?
faq.answer: There is a limited free tier. Full access to the soundscapes is a subscription, and the Australian price is not published on their site, so check the app store.

faq.question: How is it different from a playlist?
faq.answer: The sound is generated continuously rather than assembled from tracks, so it does not end, repeat or change abruptly — which is the point if you are using it to concentrate or sleep.

faq.question: Does it work offline?
faq.answer: Soundscapes can be used without a connection once the app has what it needs, which matters most for the sleep modes.

apps.title: MyFitnessPal
apps.tagline: The largest food database of any tracker, with the trade-offs that brings.
apps.excerpt: A food and exercise diary with an enormous database of foods and branded products, macro tracking and syncing with most fitness apps and wearables. It suits somebody who has been told to track what they eat, or who wants to understand their intake for a defined period.
apps.free_trial: Premium is advertised with a free trial; check the current terms in the app
apps.pricing_notes: Logging works without paying. Several features sit behind Premium, and which ones has changed over the years, so check what is included now rather than going on what you remember.
apps.take: The database is why people use it: almost anything you eat in Australia is already in there, including supermarket products. That is also its weakness — much of the data is entered by other users and some of it is wrong. Useful for a defined stretch of paying attention. Daily calorie counting does not suit everybody, and if tracking food has been difficult for you before, this is not the app to start with.
features: A very large food database, including branded and supermarket items
Barcode scanning for packaged food
Macro as well as energy tracking
Syncs with most wearables and fitness apps
pros: Almost everything you eat is already in the database
Works on the web as well as the phone
Connects to nearly everything else you might already use
cons: Much of the database is user-submitted, and some entries are wrong
Which features are free has changed repeatedly over the years
Daily calorie counting does not suit everyone, and can become its own preoccupation

faq.question: Is MyFitnessPal free?
faq.answer: Food and exercise logging works on the free tier. A number of features sit behind Premium, and which ones has changed over the years, so check what is included before subscribing.

faq.question: How accurate is the food database?
faq.answer: Mixed. Verified entries are reliable; a great many are submitted by other users and are not checked. Prefer entries marked as verified where there is a choice.

faq.question: Is calorie counting right for me?
faq.answer: That is a question for you and, if it is relevant, a dietitian or GP. Tracking suits some people for a defined period and suits others not at all.

apps.title: Easy Diet Diary
apps.tagline: An Australian food diary, free and without advertising.
apps.excerpt: Made in Brisbane by Xyris, with a food database built on Australian nutrient data and local supermarket products rather than American ones. Free, ad-free, and able to share a diary with a dietitian through the company's web tools.
apps.pricing_notes: Free, with no advertising. Xyris makes its money from professional nutrition software rather than from the app, which is why there is nothing to upgrade to.
apps.take: The obvious choice over an American tracker if you shop in Australian supermarkets, because the database is built on Australian data and local products rather than approximations of them. Free with no ads and nothing to upgrade to, which is rare enough to be worth saying twice. Plainer than the big international apps, which is mostly a virtue.
features: An Australian food database with local branded products
Barcode scanning for packaged food
Energy in kilojoules or calories, plus macronutrients
Shares a diary with a dietitian through Xyris's web tools
pros: Australian data rather than converted American figures
Genuinely free, with no ads and no upgrade
Used by dietitians here, so a practitioner can work from it
cons: Plainer and fewer features than the large international trackers
Little use if you eat mostly food bought outside Australia

faq.question: Is Easy Diet Diary really free?
faq.answer: Yes — free, with no advertising and no paid tier. Xyris sells professional nutrition software, which is what funds it.

faq.question: Why use it instead of MyFitnessPal?
faq.answer: The food database is Australian, so supermarket products and nutrient figures match what you actually buy rather than an American equivalent.

faq.question: Can my dietitian see my diary?
faq.answer: Yes, if you choose to share it. That is done through Xyris's web tools, which a number of Australian dietitians already use.

apps.title: Yuka
apps.tagline: Scan a barcode and get a rating for the product, with an alternative suggested.
apps.excerpt: Scans food and cosmetics in the supermarket and gives each product a score out of a hundred, with a short explanation and a suggested alternative where the score is poor. Free, independent, and carries no advertising — and the scoring is its own, not an official standard.
apps.pricing_notes: Scanning is free and there is no advertising. An optional paid tier adds offline scanning and history; the company publishes how it makes its money on its own site.
apps.take: Useful as a way of reading a label without reading a label, particularly for additives you would otherwise have to look up in the aisle. Treat the score as one opinion rather than a verdict: the method is Yuka's own, it weighs things in a particular way, and nutritionists disagree with parts of it. Good for noticing what is in something; less good as the only thing you decide with.
features: Barcode scanning for food and personal care products
A score with a plain-language explanation of why
Suggested alternatives when a product scores badly
No advertising, and no brand able to influence a rating
pros: Fast way to see what is actually in a packaged product
Independent of the brands it rates
Free to use, with the business model published
cons: The scoring method is Yuka's own and is not universally agreed with
Australian product coverage is thinner than in Europe
A single number can flatten a more complicated picture

faq.question: Is Yuka free?
faq.answer: Yes, for scanning. There is an optional paid tier for offline use and history, and no advertising in the app.

faq.question: Is the score reliable?
faq.answer: It is Yuka's own method, weighted its own way, and nutrition professionals disagree with parts of it. It is a useful prompt to read the label rather than a substitute for advice.

faq.question: Does it work on Australian products?
faq.answer: Many, but coverage here is thinner than in Europe, where the app started. Unrecognised products can be added by users.

apps.title: Oak
apps.tagline: Free meditation and breathing, with nothing held back and nothing to buy.
apps.excerpt: A small, free app with guided and unguided meditation, a few breathing exercises and a streak counter — and no subscription, no account and no upsell. It suits somebody who wants to try meditating without first deciding which subscription to trial.
apps.pricing_notes: Free, with no subscription and nothing held back behind one.
apps.take: The least demanding way to find out whether meditating suits you: no account, no trial to remember to cancel, and a timer that does not want anything from you. The library is small and that is the trade — if you want a course to follow, this is not it. Worth knowing it is updated less often than the larger apps.
features: Guided mindfulness and loving-kindness meditations
Unguided sessions with a timer and optional background sound
Breathing exercises alongside the meditations
A streak counter, without notifications nagging you
pros: Genuinely free with nothing behind a subscription
No account needed, so nothing to cancel or unsubscribe from
Small enough not to be overwhelming on the first day
cons: iPhone only — there is no Android version
A small library with no structured course to work through
Updated less often than the larger meditation apps

faq.question: Is Oak completely free?
faq.answer: Yes. There is no subscription and no paid tier, and you do not need to create an account.

faq.question: Is Oak on Android?
faq.answer: No. It is an iPhone app. Smiling Mind and Insight Timer are the closest free alternatives on Android.

faq.question: Is it enough on its own?
faq.answer: For finding out whether meditation suits you, yes. If you want a structured course to follow week by week, a larger app will serve you better.
